claims.text: Switching from conventional casting to powder metallurgy with controlled sintering increases the coercive field of a magnetic high-entropy alloy.
The conventionally cast baseline has a relatively coarse grain structure.
Powder metallurgy produces a finer microstructure than conventional casting.
Powder metallurgy increases the density of grain boundaries and microstructural defects such as dislocations and fine precipitates.
Refined grain boundaries and microstructural defects act as pinning sites for magnetic domain walls.
Increasing the number and effectiveness of domain-wall pinning sites hinders domain-wall motion.
Hindered domain-wall motion increases the coercive field.
The coercive field of powder-metallurgy samples will exceed that of composition-matched conventionally cast samples.
The predicted coercivity increase requires the alloy composition to remain constant between processing routes.
The predicted effect depends on controlling particle size, sintering temperature, and sintering time.
The coercivity increase is expected only at temperatures where the alloy retains magnetic order.
Excessive grain-boundary effects could adversely affect the alloy's magnetic ordering.
The effect should hold under magnetic-field and temperature conditions typical of the alloy's operational range.
Increased domain-wall pinning may trade off against reductions in saturation magnetization.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase is sensitive to the specific sintering conditions.
